Corfu New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Kerkira, Greece

Not demolished. A Romaniot Jewish community formed in Corfu during the Middle Ages, joined in the late 14th century by southern Italian Jews and, following the Spanish/Portuguese/Sicilian expulsions, by Sephardi refugees; population reached about 200 families by 1522. The Italian congregation grew from 1540-41, including exile Yitzhak Abravanel, who wrote his Isaiah commentary there before moving to Venice; three synagogues operated by then. A 1622 ghetto decree still afforded government protection, and the Romaniot community preserved a distinct Greek tradition known as the Corfu Rite. Early 19th-century growth continued with Italian and Ottoman immigrants; population reached 1,229 (of 45,000 total) by 1802, further swelled by Romaniot refugees fleeing the Greek War of Independence in the 1820s-30s, alongside modernized Jewish education. Population peaked at 6,000 (of 64,974 total) by 1863; a Hebrew press operated intermittently 1853-1896, with girls' (1875) and elementary (1887) schools following, supported by international Jewish philanthropy (Alliance Israelite, the Hirsch and Rothschild families) after anti-Jewish riots. Greece's second Zionist organization formed in 1906; population fell to about 3,000 by 1923 (4th largest in Greece). Prewar population reached 1,880, two-thirds Italian and one-third Greek congregations, the former maintaining three synagogues to the latter's one. German bombing in 1943 destroyed many Jewish homes and all three Italian synagogues; about 1,800 Jews were deported by freight train to Auschwitz in May 1944, with few surviving. Postwar recovery, joined by about 120 refugees from elsewhere, kept the community small (85-125 members through the late 1940s-50s). This newer cemetery's founding is unknown, presumed 19th-20th century.
